subject: Re: Order Form & MSA — uptime floor and maintenance carve-outs
messages:
From: Oliver Grant <oliver@aurorahealth.ai>
To: marissa.cole@redwood.com
Cc: legal@aurorahealth.ai
Date: Tue, 17 Nov 2026 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: MSA/Order Form redlines — uptime floor & maintenance carve-outs

Marissa,

Thanks again for the demo last week — Aurora is excited about Redwood’s runtime and the predictability you showed for our bursty workloads. Our procurement and legal teams reviewed the MSA + Order Form and attached a redline set (Aurora_MSA_v3_redlines.pdf). A few high-level items we need clarified before we can move to signatures: 

- Uptime floor: we need a 99.99% uptime floor across the Hosted API for production endpoints (we consider downtime to include failed inference responses and regional service degradation).
- Maintenance carve-outs: Aurora wants scheduled maintenance and planned capacity upgrades to be explicitly excluded from downtime calculations, but only with a 30-day notification and a hard cap of 72 hours per calendar year.
- Emergency maintenance: Aurora will not accept unlimited emergency maintenance carve-outs — we propose a 4-hour notice window where feasible, and no more than 48 hours of emergency maintenance credited per year.
- Service credits: if uptime falls below the floor, we propose a sliding credit scale starting at 10% monthly credit when below 99.99% down to 40% if <99.5%.
- Response times: P1 response SLA of 2 hours and P2 of 4 hours (we will coordinate incident classification).

We flagged these as material to our BOM and clinical-availability committees. Can Redwood provide counterproposals on notification cadence, credit caps, and whether maintenance windows can be scheduled outside Aurora’s core hours (M–F 06:00–18:00 PT)?

Attached: Aurora_MSA_v3_redlines.pdf (redline), uptime_matrix_v2.xlsx (Aurora’s proposed credit math).

Regards,
Oliver Grant
Head of Platform Procurement
Aurora Health

---

Oliver — thanks for the clear write-up and the attachments. Really appreciate the level of detail from Aurora’s side. I’ve pulled in Ben (Sales) to coordinate negotiation terms and Rishi + Irene for technical and legal inputs respectively.

High-level next steps from Redwood:
- I’ll run a quick internal ops feasibility check on the 99.99% floor vs. 99.95% and follow up with observed p95/p99 latency and regional fail-over behavior by EOD Wednesday.
- Rishi, can you map Aurora’s uptime definition to our monitoring (what constitutes ‘failed inference responses’ vs. degraded latency)? We want to avoid ambiguous triggers that could create spurious credits.
- Irene, please review Aurora’s suggested credit ladder and the 30-day notification / 72-hour scheduled maintenance cap. Flag must-haves vs. items we can compromise on.

Oliver — would you be available for a 30-min alignment call Thursday 10–10:30am PT? Ben will send a calendar invite if that works. We’d prefer to settle the Order Form SLA language and then route a short redline to legal for final pass.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.com
+1 415-555-0192

From: rishi.malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>
To: marissa.cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, ben.carter@redwood.com
Cc: marissa.cole@redwood.com, irene.choi@redwood.com
Date: Wed, 18 Nov 2026 09:24:00 -0800
Subject: Re: MSA/Order Form redlines — uptime floor & maintenance carve-outs

Marissa / Ben — quick technical note before the call:

1) Uptime baseline — Our production telemetry across 2026 shows median monthly availability of 99.976% across multi-region clusters for inference endpoints (global synthetic checks + customer telemetry). We can push to a contractual 99.95% uptime comfortably with standard redundancy; 99.99% materially increases cost and operational constraints (more reserved capacity, stricter over-provisioning).

2) Maintenance windows — We prefer scheduled maintenance to be excluded from uptime, but request that Aurora accept a standard model:
   - Up to 120 hours of scheduled maintenance per year may be excluded if communicated 14 days in advance and scheduled outside Aurora’s declared business hours unless Aurora explicitly requests otherwise.
   - For emergency maintenance (security hotpatches, CVEs), allow exclusions with best-effort 4-hour notice; we measure emergency events and propose a 48-hour annual cap (agreed events beyond that roll into credit math).

3) Service credit ladder — Rishi suggests a capped monthly credit program:
   - 99.95–99.80% => 10% credit
   - 99.79–99.50% => 20% credit
   - <99.50% => 40% credit, capped at 3 months of fees per rolling 12 months

4) Definition clarification — We must define whether partial-region degradation (e.g., us-west region latency spikes but global fallback succeeds) counts as downtime for Aurora’s endpoints. My recommendation: downtime is when requests for an endpoint fail (5xx) or exceed hard latency threshold X (we should define X per API). Otherwise, region-level latency increases are operational alerts, not automatic credits.

I’ll prepare a short excerpt for the Order Form that maps our telemetry metrics to the definitions. Marissa — I’ll drop that into the shared Doc before the call.

—Rishi

Subject: Re: MSA/Order Form redlines — uptime floor & maintenance carve-outs

Marissa / Ben — thanks for routing. A few counterpoints from Aurora legal and clinical risk: 

- 99.99% requirement is non-negotiable for production clinical inference that impacts live patient triage — a single hour of downtime in peak results in unacceptable clinical risk profiles for our deployments.
- The 72-hour scheduled maintenance cap is acceptable only if emergency maintenance is strictly limited; our legal counsel will not accept unlimited emergency carve-outs for security patches without near-immediate notification.
- 30-day notification for scheduled maintenance is our minimum for planning; anything shorter will be escalated internally.
- Service credit scale: Aurora is willing to accept caps on cumulative credits, but insists on a minimum floor of 15% monthly credit for incidents below 99.99%.

We can accept a technical definition that differentiates full endpoint failure from latency-based degradations, but Aurora’s clinical team requires that any degradation leading to >10% request failure rate over a 30-minute window be treated as downtime for SLA purposes.

Please propose a written compromise (Order Form language) that we can circulate via DocuSign for signatures once both sides agree.

Regards,
Aurora Health Legal
legal@aurorahealth.ai

Attachment(s): none
